plan.theme: whether public libraries should lend tools, equipment and other practical objects as well as books

payload.title: Synthesis: Should Public Libraries Lend Tools and Equipment as Well as Books?

prompt.scenario: A growing number of public libraries now lend objects other than books and media: power drills, sewing machines, cake pans, camping gear, energy meters, musical instruments. Supporters call these collections a natural extension of what a library has always done. Critics worry about cost, maintenance, liability and the dilution of a library's core purpose. Others argue that such lending is worthwhile only under certain conditions, or that other institutions are better suited to the job. Carefully read the six sources that follow, including the introductory information for each source.
prompt.task: Write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether public libraries should lend tools, equipment and other practical objects in addition to books.
requirements: Take a clear, defensible position on the question; a conditional or limited position is acceptable if it is clearly stated and consistently argued.
Use material from at least three of the six sources to support your reasoning, and attribute each source as Source A, Source B, Source C, Source D, Source E or Source F.
Treat the sources as evidence for your own argument rather than as a list to summarize; explain how each piece of evidence supports or complicates your position.
Address at least one reasonable objection to your position, drawing on a source that disagrees with you where possible.

sources.title: Check Out a Drill
sources.attribution: Lenora Vasquez-Pryor, opinion column in The Harrowgate Ledger, 2025
sources.body:
Last spring my neighbor needed to hang a storm door. He does not own a drill. A decent one costs more than a week of groceries for his family, and he needed it for about forty minutes. He walked four blocks to the Marrowfield Public Library and came home with a cordless drill, a level and a box of bits, on loan for a week, for nothing.

This is not a gimmick. It is the oldest idea a library has, pointed at a new kind of object. A library has always been the place where a town pools what no single household can justify buying and lets everyone use it in turn. In 1890 that meant an encyclopedia. In 1990 it meant a videotape. Today it can mean a sewing machine, and in the Pellridge cooperative, sewing machines alone went out 2,300 times last year.

The critics say books are the mission. But the mission was never paper. The mission was access: to knowledge, to skill, to the ability to fix your own porch step instead of paying someone or leaving it broken. A borrowed drill teaches a teenager that she can repair things. A borrowed energy meter shows a renter which old refrigerator is draining the bill. Those are lessons, and a library that will lend a book about carpentry but not a hammer has stopped halfway.

Will some items break? Of course. Books get coffee on them too. We did not stop lending books. We should not flinch now because a drill battery costs more than a paperback. What the drill returns to the town is worth more than what it costs the shelf.

sources.title: Memorandum on Non-Traditional Lending Collections
sources.attribution: Castlebrook Library Board of Trustees, internal policy memo to the town finance committee, 2025
sources.body:
Purpose. The finance committee has asked whether the Castlebrook Public Library should expand its collection of tools, kitchen equipment and outdoor gear. The board recommends that it should not, and that the existing collection be held at its current size pending review.

Cost. In 2025 the non-book collection consumed 3.8 percent of the library's operating budget while producing 3.1 percent of total circulation. Books and media remain far cheaper per loan. A paperback is repaired with tape; a tent is returned with a torn fly and a missing pole, and someone must inventory it, order the part and decide whether to bill the patron.

Staff. Our circulation desk is staffed by two part-time clerks. Checking in a pressure washer is not like checking in a novel. It must be inspected, cleaned, tested and, if it fails, pulled from the catalog. Over the past year, staff logged roughly 140 hours on object maintenance, hours not spent on reference questions, children's programs or shelving.

Liability. The board has received one letter from a patron who cut his hand using a borrowed jigsaw. No claim was filed, but counsel has advised that a signed waiver does not eliminate the town's exposure. We lend books without worrying that a reader will be injured by them.

Mission. The board is not opposed in principle to lending useful objects. We are opposed to doing it badly, with no dedicated funding, in a building with one storage closet. A small library that tries to be a hardware store will become a mediocre hardware store and a worse library. If the town wants a tool collection, it should fund one directly and house it elsewhere.

sources.title: Five Questions for Odalys Brenner, Director of the Marrowfield Public Library
sources.attribution: Interview excerpt published in Shelf Notes, the newsletter of the Pellridge Regional Library Cooperative, 2025
sources.body:
Shelf Notes: Marrowfield has lent tools since 2021. Has it worked?

Brenner: By the numbers, yes. Our objects are about 2 percent of our budget and over 4 percent of our checkouts. Roughly a third of the new library cards we issued last year were to adults who came in for a drill or a sewing machine and had not had a card since childhood. Some of them now borrow books. That matters to me more than the circulation count.

Shelf Notes: What would you tell a library that wants to start?

Brenner: Do not pay for it out of the book budget. Our first 200 items came from a two-year grant from the Tollan Family Foundation, and a local credit union still covers repairs. Without that money I would not have started. Second, train staff before the first loan goes out. We spent a month learning how to test a battery and spot a dull blade. Third, choose items by upkeep, not by excitement. Cake pans and energy meters almost never break. Camping gear comes back wet. Instruments need a technician. We lend all of them, but we lend far more of the first kind.

Shelf Notes: What has gone wrong?

Brenner: Waiting lists. Our most popular sewing machine has a hold queue of seven weeks. People who needed it to hem a uniform for a job interview could not wait, and that bothers me, because they are exactly the people we meant to serve. We also had two items stolen in the first year. Both were replaced, but the staff felt it.

Shelf Notes: So should every library do this?

Brenner: No. Every library should ask what its town cannot afford to own one at a time, and whether the library is the right place to hold it. For us the answer was yes. For a library with one clerk and no closet, the honest answer might be no.

sources.title: Letter to the Editor: Leave the Tools to People Who Know Them
sources.attribution: Gunnar Halvorsen, owner of Halvorsen Rental and Supply, letter published in The Dunmere Courier, 2024
sources.body:
To the editor:

I have rented tools in Dunmere for twenty-six years. I am writing because the library board is considering a tool collection, and I want to say plainly what I think, since people will assume I am only protecting my business. I am partly protecting my business. I am also right.

When a man rents a tile saw from me, I ask what he is cutting. I show him where the guard goes. I tell him the blade is wet-cut and will throw water. If he comes back with the fence bent, I know, because I set it that morning. A library clerk who is also handling a story hour and a printer jam cannot do that, and no training month will make her a tradesman. The result will be injured amateurs and tools that quietly go dull, because no one on staff can feel the difference.

There is also the matter of fairness. My shop pays property tax. Part of that tax funds the library. I would be funding a competitor that charges nothing and answers to no one about its losses.

I am not against people borrowing tools. Here is what I would support. Let the library keep a list of what I and the other two shops in town carry, and send people to us. Let the town pay for a voucher program for residents who cannot afford a rental; I will honor it. Let the library lend the small things, the cake pans and the meters, that no shop bothers with. And let the community college, which already has a shop and an instructor, run a tool loan for anyone who takes its free safety class.

The library is good at what it does. So am I. Nobody gains when we swap jobs.

Gunnar Halvorsen, Dunmere

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that merely restates the question (libraries lending tools has pros and cons), or a thesis that only summarizes what the sources say without taking a position. A thesis that answers a different question (for example, whether libraries should exist) also earns 0.
descriptors.1: States a defensible position on whether public libraries should lend practical objects. The position may be a full yes, a full no, a conditional stance (yes if funded by grants or partnerships; yes for low-upkeep items only; yes only once a waiting-list problem is solved), or an alternative stance (other institutions should do it). The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay but must be a claim, not a plan of organization.

rows.task_specific: A thesis such as 'Libraries should lend tools because access, not paper, is the mission' earns the point. 'Libraries should lend some objects but not others, judged by upkeep cost' earns the point. 'Lending tools is good but also has drawbacks' does not, because it takes no position.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, offers only personal opinion with no reference to the sources, or references sources without any relation to a position.
descriptors.1: Uses fewer than three sources, or uses three or more sources only through summary or quotation dropped in without explanation. The essay reads as a tour of the sources (Source A says, Source B says) rather than an argument.
descriptors.2: Draws on at least three sources with evidence that is relevant to the thesis, but commentary is thin or repetitive: the writer asserts that a source supports the claim without explaining how, or the explanation simply paraphrases the source. Evidence from the table or chart is reported as numbers without interpretation.
descriptors.3: Draws on at least three sources with specific evidence, and commentary explains how most pieces of evidence support the writer's line of reasoning. The essay has a line of reasoning that moves beyond listing. Some evidence may be loosely connected or one source may be mischaracterized, and the quantitative sources may be used somewhat superficially.
descriptors.4: Draws on at least three sources with specific, well-chosen evidence, and every piece of evidence is explained in relation to a clear line of reasoning. The writer integrates sources with one another (for example, uses the upkeep figures in Source E to test the budget concern in Source B, or reads the Castlebrook bars in Source F against Marrowfield's bars). Opposing sources are engaged rather than ignored, and the writer explains why the objection does not overturn the position or how it narrows it.

rows.task_specific: Count a source as used only if the writer draws specific content from it (a claim, a figure, an example) and connects it to the argument. A bare citation tag with no content does not count. For a score of 4, expect at least one place where two sources are put in conversation and at least one place where a number from Source E or F is interpreted (what it suggests, what it does not show) rather than merely quoted. Misreading a source (for example, claiming Source C opposes tool lending) caps the row at 2 unless the rest of the evidence is strong, in which case cap at 3.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Argument stays at the level of general assertion; complexity is gestured at ('there are many sides') but not developed; style is competent but unremarkable, or ornate in ways that hide rather than sharpen the argument.
descriptors.1: The essay demonstrates thoughtful complexity in at least one sustained way: it identifies tensions within the evidence (circulation share versus budget share; high loans but high upkeep for some categories), it recognizes the limits of its own position (which items, which towns, which funding), it situates the question in a broader context (what a public institution is for; who is served by a collection), or it is written with a consistently controlled, precise and persuasive style throughout.

rows.task_specific: Award the point for essays that, for example, distinguish between item categories using Source E (cake pans at 6 dollars upkeep versus instruments at 57) to build a conditional position, or that notice the Castlebrook outlier in Source F and explain what it implies for the budget objection, or that question whether circulation counts are the right measure of a library's value. Do not award for a single sentence of hedging or a concluding flourish.

scoring_notes: A response that argues against tool lending is fully able to earn 6 points; the rubric rewards reasoning, not the side chosen.
Sources B and D are the main counter-evidence; a high-scoring essay that argues for lending should engage at least one of them.

The table (Source E) and the chart (Source F) share no identical quantities with each other, but Sources A, B and C cite figures that match them; writers who notice and use these matches should be credited for integration.
Do not penalize a writer for using only three sources if those three are used well; do not reward a writer for naming all six if the uses are shallow.

defensible_positions: Libraries should lend practical objects broadly because access, not format, is the library's purpose and the data show strong demand (Sources A, C, E, F).
Libraries should not expand into object lending because per-loan costs, staff time and liability undermine the core service, especially in small libraries (Sources B, D, F Castlebrook bars).
Libraries should lend objects only under conditions: dedicated outside funding, trained staff and a focus on low-upkeep categories such as kitchen equipment and meters (Sources C, E, D's concession).

Object lending is worthwhile but should be shared with or handed to other institutions, such as rental shops through vouchers or a community college workshop, while the library lends only small items (Source D with support from B).
Whether to lend objects depends on the individual town: libraries should decide by their own size, storage and demand rather than by a blanket rule (Sources C, F).
lines_of_reasoning: Equity of access: objects used rarely but needed urgently are exactly what shared ownership is for; the loan counts in Source E show real demand.
Cost-benefit by category: Source E's upkeep column lets a writer separate cheap, high-demand items from expensive, low-demand ones and build a selective policy.
Institutional fit: Sources B, C and D all raise whether a library has the staff, space and expertise; a writer can argue fit is the deciding factor rather than principle.
Outcomes beyond circulation: Source C's point about new cardholders lets a writer argue that value is not captured by budget-versus-circulation comparisons alone.
Second-order effects: Source D's fairness argument and Source C's waiting lists suggest that even successful programs create new problems that a position must address.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Source A opens with a neighbor's storm door to make the abstract idea of access concrete and to show that need can be brief but real.
Source A links the encyclopedia, the videotape and the sewing machine to argue that object lending is continuous with library history.
Source B contrasts a taped paperback with a torn tent to make the maintenance burden vivid for the finance committee.
Source D admits self-interest before asserting correctness, buying credibility for the expertise argument that follows.
Source C lays out three numbered conditions, which a writer can adopt as the structure of a conditional position.

source_uses.usable_for: Framing access as the library's mission; the storm-door anecdote; the 2,300 sewing-machine loans figure (matches Source E); the claim that breakage is no more disqualifying for tools than for books.

Cost, staffing and liability objections; the Castlebrook 3.8 percent budget versus 3.1 percent circulation figures (match Source F); the 140 staff hours; the proposal to fund and house a collection elsewhere; its concession that it is not opposed in principle.

Evidence that programs can succeed (2 percent of budget, over 4 percent of checkouts, matching Source F); the new-cardholder effect; the conditions of outside funding, training and low-upkeep selection; the waiting-list and theft problems; the claim that not every library should do this.

Expertise and safety objection; the fairness argument about taxpayer-funded competition; alternative models (vouchers, referral lists, community college loan); its concession that libraries could lend small items.

Comparing demand across categories (tools 6,850 loans; instruments 1,180); comparing upkeep (cake pans 6 dollars; instruments 57 dollars); showing that the most widely lent categories are the cheapest to maintain; supporting a selective or conditional stance.

Showing that in four of five libraries objects deliver more circulation share than budget share; identifying Castlebrook as the exception that supports Source B; arguing that results depend on the particular library rather than on the idea itself.

common_pitfalls: Treating the question as pro or con only and ignoring the possibility of a conditional stance, so that the essay cannot account for the mixed evidence in Sources C, E and F.
Summarizing each source in order rather than building a line of reasoning and pulling evidence where it is needed.
Quoting numbers from Source E or F without saying what they show; for instance, reporting that tools were borrowed 6,850 times without connecting that figure to access, cost or demand.
Mischaracterizing Source C as opposed to object lending because the director mentions problems; her stance is conditional support.
Ignoring Source D entirely because it is a letter from a business owner, or dismissing it as self-interested without addressing the liability and expertise arguments it raises.
Writing a thesis about whether libraries matter in general rather than about lending practical objects.

plan.theme: a retiring ferry captain's address to a river town about the patience that safe crossings require

payload.title: Rhetorical Analysis: Captain Ines Marrow's Farewell Address at Birch Landing

prompt.scenario: Speaker: Ines Marrow, a ferry captain retiring after thirty-one years piloting the crossing of the Tessel River between the towns of Birch Landing and Ferris Point. Audience: residents of Birch Landing gathered at the town's annual Landing Day celebration, including daily commuters who have often been inconvenienced by her refusals to sail, and the unnamed successor who will take the wheel. Exigence: her last night as captain; the town has a history of grumbling about delayed crossings, and she wants to leave behind a way of thinking about those delays before she goes. Purpose: to persuade the town that waiting is an act of skill and care rather than timidity, and to shape how they treat the next captain.
prompt.task: The passage below is adapted from remarks delivered in 2019 by Ines Marrow, a ferry captain retiring after thirty-one years on the Tessel River crossing, to the residents of the river town of Birch Landing at their annual Landing Day gathering. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Marrow makes to convince her neighbors that the patience required for safe crossings is a form of care rather than weakness.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of how Marrow's rhetorical choices serve her purpose.
Select and cite specific evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
Explain in your commentary how the evidence you cite demonstrates the way particular choices advance Marrow's purpose with this audience.

sources.title: Remarks at Landing Day
sources.attribution: Ines Marrow, retiring captain of the Tessel River ferry, address to the town of Birch Landing, 2019
paragraphs: (1) Thirty-one years ago this October, I stood on the deck of the old Corwin for the first time, nineteen years old, wearing a borrowed coat and holding no idea how long a river could make a person wait.
(2) Tonight I am giving that deck back to you.
(3) Before I do, I want to tell you what the Tessel taught me, because most of it was not about boats.
(4) People think a ferry captain's job is to go.
(5) It is not.
(6) A ferry captain's job is to know when not to go.
(7) I have counted, roughly, and in thirty-one years I have made something close to forty thousand crossings.
(8) I have also refused about six hundred.

(9) Six hundred mornings when the fog sat on the water like a lid on a pot, or the current came down brown and fast from the hills, and I turned to a dock full of people with somewhere to be and said the one word nobody wants to hear from the only person who could carry them across: wait.
(10) I know what that word costs.
(11) It costs the nurse her shift at the county hospital, the farmer his place in line at the grain scale, the boy his first day of school on the other bank.
(12) I have heard every argument you have, and some of them were good.

(13) In the spring of my fourth season a man named Dell Ambrose stood at the rail with his wife in labor in the back of his truck and told me, quietly, that he would never forgive me if I kept the boat tied.
(14) I kept it tied.
(15) Forty minutes later the fog lifted, we crossed, and the baby was born at the hospital in Ferris Point with both parents alive to argue about her name.
(16) I do not tell that story to make myself the hero of it.
(17) I tell it because those forty minutes were the longest stretch of my life, and I would choose them again.
(18) Here is the thing about a river: it does not negotiate.
(19) You can argue with a schedule, you can argue with a boss, you can even argue with me, and some of you have, loudly.
(20) The Tessel does not hear you.
(21) It keeps its own hours, and it keeps them without apology.
(22) The only power a captain has is the power to match the river's hours instead of pretending she can outrun them.
(23) Now, I will grant you that patience can be a disguise for timidity.
(24) There were surely mornings I could have gone and did not, and somebody lost a day they did not need to lose.
(25) I am not asking you to admire a woman who was afraid of her own river.
(26) But between the captain who waits one hour too long and the captain who leaves five minutes too early, only one of them ever has to stand up in a church and explain herself.
(27) I have attended that kind of service in other towns.
(28) I never had to host one here.
(29) So this is what I am leaving on the deck for whoever takes the wheel next, and for the rest of you too, because you do not need a ferry to find yourself staring at something you cannot hurry.
(30) Patience is not standing still.
(31) Patience is reading the water while you stand.

(32) It is the fog, and the current, and the long gray minute when everyone on the dock is looking at the back of your head, and you decide, again, that getting there matters less than getting there whole.
(33) Birch Landing, you have been a good crowd to keep waiting.
(34) You brought me coffee in the fog.
(35) You forgave me, mostly.
(36) The next time the horn does not sound at seven, I hope you will remember that silence is sometimes the sound of somebody taking care of you.
(37) Thank you for the crossings, all of them, including the ones we did not make.
sources.stance: Waiting to cross is an act of judgment and care, not fear.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Marrow uses many rhetorical choices to convince the town that patience is care'), or a statement that summarizes the speech without claiming anything about how its choices work, or a claim about the topic of patience itself rather than about the passage.
descriptors.1: A defensible claim about how Marrow's choices work on this audience. It may name specific strategies (the Ambrose anecdote, the personified river, the admission that patience can hide timidity) or it may characterize her overall approach (for instance, that she reframes the town's grievance as evidence of her care). The thesis need not preview three devices; it must make an arguable claim the essay can develop.

rows.task_specific: Award the point for any thesis that connects at least one identifiable choice or pattern in the passage to Marrow's purpose of redefining waiting as care. A thesis that reads her purpose as merely 'saying goodbye' is too thin; a thesis that reads it as 'defending her record against grumblers' or 'preparing the town for her successor' is acceptable because the passage supports both.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the speech, or offers evidence that has nothing to do with the claim.
descriptors.1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of the passage with a few general references ('she tells a story about a baby'). Any commentary is a label ('this is pathos') with no explanation of effect.
descriptors.2: Quotes or cites specific sentences and attaches commentary, but the commentary is generic or repeated (every paragraph ends with 'this makes the audience trust her'). The essay may list devices without linking them to one another or to the purpose. Identification is accurate but explanation of how the choice works on this particular audience is thin.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence from several parts of the passage, with commentary that explains how at least two choices work and ties them to the purpose of reframing waiting as care. Some commentary may be uneven or one piece of evidence may be left unexplained, and the line of reasoning may be present but not fully built from paragraph to paragraph.
descriptors.4: Specific, well-chosen evidence throughout, with commentary that consistently explains how each cited choice advances Marrow's purpose with this audience, and a line of reasoning that develops across the essay (for example, moving from how she establishes authority through the numbers, to how the anecdote makes the cost of waiting concrete, to how the concession in paragraph five disarms the charge of cowardice, to how the closing redefines silence). The essay explains why the choice matters to residents who have been inconvenienced, not just what the choice is.

rows.task_specific: Choices that count include: the statistic of forty thousand crossings against six hundred refusals (sentences 7 to 8); the simile of fog like a lid on a pot and the colon isolating 'wait' (9); the tricolon of nurse, farmer, boy (11); the Dell Ambrose anecdote and the short sentence 'I kept it tied' (13 to 17); the personified, non-negotiating river (18 to 22); the concession and rebuttal about timidity and the church service (23 to 28); the redefinition of patience (30 to 32); the direct address and understatement of 'You forgave me, mostly' (33 to 35); the closing paradox about silence (36). Credit any accurately described choice whose effect is explained; do not require the student to use the device names in the inventory. Commentary that explains the anecdote only as 'emotional' without noting that Marrow refuses hero status (16) and so turns it into an argument about judgment should be capped at a 2 for that piece of evidence.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Commentary stays at the level of identification plus effect, or the essay gestures at complexity with vague phrases ('this adds depth') without earning it. Ornate vocabulary alone does not earn the point.
descriptors.1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained, specific way: explains how the choices interact (for instance, how the concession in paragraph five depends on the credibility built by the numbers in paragraph two); accounts for the shift from the stern, river-does-not-negotiate voice to the tender final paragraph and what that shift does for an audience that has resented her; identifies a tension in the speech (she disclaims hero status while telling a story in which she is plainly right) and explains how it serves her; or situates the speech in its occasion, noting that she is speaking as much to her successor and to the town's future treatment of that successor as about herself. The prose is controlled and precise.

rows.task_specific: The strongest sophistication arguments will notice that Marrow's audience is also her accuser: the people she kept waiting are the ones she thanks. Essays that explain how she converts the town's grievance into a shared record of safe arrivals, or that read 'the ones we did not make' as the thesis of the whole speech, should earn this point if the explanation is developed rather than asserted.

scoring_notes: Score holistically within Row B; do not deduct for a single misidentified device if the overall commentary is sound.

An essay that reads the passage as a eulogy or as an argument about river safety regulations has misread the occasion; its thesis may still earn Row A if defensible, but Row B is likely capped at 2 because commentary will not connect to the actual purpose.
Do not reward a five-paragraph device inventory (ethos, pathos, logos) over an essay that traces two choices thoroughly; the latter typically scores higher in Row B.
Quotation is not required; precise paraphrase with sentence reference counts as specific evidence.
Row C can be earned by an essay that scores 3 in Row B if the sophistication is genuine; it should rarely be earned by an essay scoring 2 or lower.

defensible_positions: Marrow builds credibility through concrete numbers and a single vivid refusal, then uses that credibility to redefine the town's complaint as proof of her care.
By personifying the river as something that will not negotiate, Marrow shifts blame for delays from herself to the water, so that waiting becomes obedience to fact rather than a captain's whim.
Marrow's concession that patience can hide timidity, followed by the image of the church service, turns the strongest objection to her record into the strongest argument for it.
The speech moves from a stern, instructive voice to a tender farewell, and that shift lets Marrow finish by asking the town to extend to her successor the forgiveness she is thanking them for.
lines_of_reasoning: Authority first (sentences 1, 7 to 8), then cost acknowledged (10 to 11), then a test case (13 to 17), then the principle (18 to 22), then the objection answered (23 to 28), then the redefinition and farewell (29 to 37).
Tracing how the single word 'wait' in sentence 9 is reframed step by step until silence becomes care in sentence 36.
Contrasting the two voices in the speech, the captain who does not negotiate and the neighbor who was brought coffee, and showing how each serves a different part of the audience's resistance.

rhetorical_choices.effect: The precise span of years and the image of the nineteen-year-old in a borrowed coat establish Marrow as someone who earned her judgment over time, making her later claims about refusals credible.
Setting 'to go' against 'when not to go' in three short sentences overturns the audience's assumption about what a captain is for, and the blunt 'It is not' gives the correction force.
Forty thousand crossings against six hundred refusals shows the audience that her caution was rare, undercutting the memory that she was always late.
Fog like a lid on a pot makes the danger domestic and visible, so the refusal seems obvious rather than fussy.
The colon isolates the single word 'wait' after a long sentence, letting the audience feel the weight of the word they resent.
The nurse, the farmer, and the boy name the audience's real losses in their own terms, proving she understood the cost before she asks them to accept it.
The Ambrose story is the hardest possible case for waiting, and by letting it end well while disclaiming hero status she turns an emotional story into an argument about judgment.
The long sentence of the husband's plea collapses into the four-word 'I kept it tied', enacting the stubbornness of the decision.
A river that does not negotiate and keeps its own hours relocates the source of delay from the captain to the water, so her refusals look like realism rather than will.
Granting that patience can be timidity, and admitting some lost days, lets her answer the objection on its strongest form with the asymmetry of the church service.
One hour too long against five minutes too early, and services attended elsewhere against none hosted here, make the stakes of error unequal and the choice obvious.
Redefining patience as reading the water rather than standing still converts the audience's image of idleness into an image of work.
The voice turns from instruction to gratitude, and the shift rewards the audience for having listened to the hard part before asking them to carry the lesson forward.
'You forgave me, mostly' admits lingering resentment with humor, disarming the people who still hold it.
Naming the town and speaking to 'you' about the next silent morning makes the request about their future behavior toward her successor.
Silence as the sound of care, and thanks for crossings never made, invert the audience's expectations one final time, sealing the redefinition.

source_uses.usable_for: All evidence for the rhetorical analysis; sentence numbers allow precise citation.

common_pitfalls: Listing devices in the order they appear without a controlling argument about how they add up.
Treating the Ambrose anecdote as pure pathos and missing that sentences 16 and 17 turn it into a claim about judgment rather than heroism.
Ignoring the concession in paragraph five, or misreading it as Marrow admitting she was wrong rather than narrowing the charge so she can answer it.
Describing the audience generically ('the reader') instead of as neighbors who have been inconvenienced by her and who will judge her successor.
Summarizing the speech's content about patience rather than analyzing how it is argued.
Quoting long stretches without explaining which words do the work.
Claiming the tone is 'nostalgic throughout' and missing the hard, declarative voice of paragraphs two and four.

blueprint.theme: Patience as skilled care rather than hesitation; a retiring ferry captain reframes the delays a town has resented.
blueprint.issue: Whether a captain's refusals to sail were caution worth honoring or timidity the town merely tolerated.
stances: Waiting is judgment and care, and the town's safe record proves it (Marrow).
Delays cost real people real things and were sometimes unnecessary (the audience's grievance, which Marrow concedes in part).

devices.function: Establishes earned authority through years of service and counted crossings.
Reverses the audience's assumption about a captain's job.
Shows refusals were rare relative to crossings.
Makes fog concrete and obviously dangerous.
Isolates the word 'wait' and the claim that the river does not negotiate.
Names the audience's costs and the things that can be argued with, in balanced series.
Evokes the human stakes of waiting.
Provides the hardest test case and converts it into an argument about judgment.
Short sentence after long one enacts the firmness of the decision.
Relocates responsibility for delay from captain to river.
Admits patience can be timidity, then answers with the asymmetry of consequences.
Contrasts unequal errors and services attended versus hosted.
Repeated 'Patience is' frames the redefinition.
Redefines patience as active reading of conditions.
Moves from stern instruction to warm gratitude.
Acknowledges lingering resentment with humor.
Turns the lesson into a request about future treatment of the next captain.
Silence as care and thanks for crossings not made invert expectations.

plan.theme: the extent to which schools should replace some homework with long-term community projects

payload.title: Worksheets or Footbridges: Homework and the Long-Term Community Project

prompt.scenario: In a column for a regional newspaper, education commentator Ines Varlow responded to a school district's decision to let a long-term community project take the place of part of students' nightly homework. Her column is reproduced below as Source A.
prompt.task: After reading the passage, write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which schools should replace some traditional homework with long-term community projects.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning; evidence may come from your reading, your experience, or your observation.
Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning, and use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

sources.title: Fluency, Experience, and the Creek Trail
sources.attribution: Ines Varlow, opinion column in the Halvering Courier-Ledger (fictional)
sources.body: When the Pell Hollow school district announced that eighth graders would spend the spring restoring a neglected creek trail instead of completing nightly worksheets, the complaints arrived before the shovels did. Parents asked how anyone would know whether their children could still factor a polynomial. The superintendent answered that a child who has spent forty hours persuading a town council to fund a footbridge has learned something no worksheet measures. Both sides, I think, are half right. Homework, at its best, is practice: the small, repetitive, private labor by which a skill becomes reliable. A community project is something else: public, slow, dependent on other people, and often a mess. The question is not which one is nobler. It is whether a school owes its students fluency, or experience, or some ratio of the two that nobody has yet agreed on, and whether that ratio should be set by the people who grade the work or by the people who live with the results.

sources.stance: Deliberately unresolved; frames the dispute as a question of proportion and of who decides, leaving room for several positions.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that merely restates the prompt (for example, 'Schools should think carefully about whether to replace homework with community projects'), or a statement that only summarizes Varlow's column, or a thesis that answers a different question (such as whether homework should exist at all) without connecting it to the replacement question.
descriptors.1: A defensible, specific claim about how far schools should go in substituting long-term community projects for traditional homework. The claim may be a full endorsement, a full rejection, or a qualified position (for instance, replacement is appropriate only in certain subjects, grade levels, or proportions, or only when particular conditions are met). The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: The thesis must take a position on extent, not just on whether community projects are good or whether homework is bad. 'Community projects teach valuable skills' is not yet a thesis; 'Community projects should replace homework only in subjects where the skill being practiced is the same skill the project demands' is. A thesis that argues the ratio should be decided locally by families and teachers rather than fixed by policy is also defensible, since the column explicitly raises the question of who decides.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the column, or offers only general statements with no evidence at all.
descriptors.1: Offers evidence that is mostly general or unrelated to the position (for example, a vague claim that 'students learn more by doing' with no specific example), and the commentary, if any, does not explain how the evidence supports the claim. Often reads as a list of opinions.
descriptors.2: Provides some specific evidence (a remembered assignment, a described project, a book or news story, an observed classroom) but the commentary is thin or repetitive, often just asserting that the example 'shows' the point. The line of reasoning may be present but is not consistently developed; paragraphs may feel interchangeable.
descriptors.3: Provides specific evidence for the position and explains how most of it supports the line of reasoning. The essay moves in a recognizable order (for example, establishing what homework is for, then what projects do, then where the two overlap or conflict). Some commentary may be uneven, or one piece of evidence may be left to speak for itself.
descriptors.4: Provides specific, well-chosen evidence and consistently explains how it supports the claim; the line of reasoning is clear and each paragraph advances it rather than repeating it. The essay treats the question of extent directly, showing where the proposed replacement should stop and why, and it engages with at least one plausible objection or complication rather than ignoring it.

rows.task_specific: Evidence may be personal (a service project that worked or collapsed, a homework routine that built or failed to build a skill), observed (a sibling's school, a local program), or drawn from reading. Evidence counts as specific when a grader can picture it: a named kind of task, a concrete outcome, a particular difficulty. Using the column as evidence is acceptable but not required; an essay that only paraphrases Varlow's creek trail example without adding anything earns at most a 2 on this row. Commentary must explain the link to extent, for instance why a given example shows that projects can replace practice in one domain but not another.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: The argument is sound but flat: it does not complicate its own position, treats homework or projects as uniformly good or bad, uses the counterargument only as a token to dismiss, or relies on sweeping generalizations and ornamental language that does not advance thought.
descriptors.1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained way, not as a single sentence: it complicates the question by distinguishing kinds of homework, kinds of projects, or kinds of students for whom the trade-off differs; it examines the hidden assumptions in the debate (for example, that fluency and experience are measurable on the same scale, or that 'the community' benefits equally from student labor); it considers the costs of its own position honestly (such as the inequity when projects depend on transportation or free afternoons); or it situates the question in a broader context about what schools are for. The prose is controlled and the voice is consistent.

rows.task_specific: A qualified thesis alone does not earn this point; the qualification must be developed. An essay that notices the column's final question about who sets the ratio, and builds an argument around it, is a strong candidate. So is an essay that argues the counterintuitive case (for example, that long projects should replace homework more in mathematics than in social studies, with reasons) and sustains it.

scoring_notes: Score the essay as a whole for row B; do not add points per paragraph.
An essay that argues against any replacement at all is fully defensible and should be scored on its evidence and reasoning, not on agreement with the column.

Essays that drift into arguing homework should be abolished entirely can still earn thesis credit if they explicitly connect that claim to community projects as the replacement; otherwise treat the thesis as off-task.
Length is not a criterion. A short essay with precise evidence and clear commentary can earn a 4 on row B.
Do not award the sophistication point for vocabulary or for a dramatic opening; award it only for complexity of thought that runs through the argument.

defensible_positions: Schools should replace a substantial share of homework with long-term community projects because sustained public work teaches persistence, communication, and civic judgment that private practice cannot.
Schools should keep most homework as it is, because repetitive practice is the only reliable way to build fluency, and projects should be added, not substituted.
Replacement is appropriate only where the skill the project demands is the same skill the homework was meant to practice (writing, measurement, research), and not where it is not.
The ratio should be decided locally by teachers, families, and students rather than fixed by district policy, because the costs of projects fall unevenly.
Projects should replace homework mainly in older grades, after fluency has been established, and sparingly in younger grades.
Long projects should replace homework more aggressively than most people assume, because much nightly homework is not practice at all but busywork, and the real loss is small.
lines_of_reasoning: Define what homework actually accomplishes when it works (fluency through repetition), then show which subjects depend on that and which do not; conclude that replacement should track that distinction.

Argue from the nature of long-term work: deadlines months away, dependence on other people, visible public results; show that these features build capacities schools claim to value but rarely assess, and therefore justify replacing a meaningful fraction of homework.
Argue from equity: projects require time, transport, and adult support that are unequally distributed, so replacement should be limited or paired with in-school time.

Argue from the question of who decides, following the column's closing line: since the people who grade the work and the people who live with it want different things, the ratio should be negotiated rather than imposed.

Argue the counterintuitive case that the subject most people would protect, mathematics, is actually where a long project (budgeting a footbridge, measuring a trail) can replace worksheets most fully, while subjects like literature depend on private, repeated reading that a project cannot substitute.

Argue from the risk of mess: the column admits projects are 'often a mess,' and a mess can be formative or merely wasteful depending on whether a teacher has time to turn it into learning; so replacement should be scaled to staffing, not to ideals.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Opens with a concrete local dispute so the abstract question has faces and stakes; students may use or extend this example.
Signals that the column will not pick a side, which models the qualified positions students are invited to take.
Defines homework as practice and projects as public, slow, dependent work, giving students two categories to accept, refine, or challenge.
Reframes the debate from nobility to proportion and authority, opening the question of who should set the ratio.

source_uses.usable_for: The creek trail and footbridge example as a concrete case; the definitions of homework as practice and projects as public and slow; the closing question about fluency versus experience and about who decides the ratio. Students may adopt, qualify, or reject Varlow's framing, but must add evidence of their own.

common_pitfalls: Arguing about whether homework is good or bad in general instead of about the extent to which projects should replace it.
Treating 'community projects' as automatically virtuous and offering no account of what students would stop practicing.
Relying entirely on Varlow's creek trail example instead of supplying evidence of one's own.
Writing a thesis that says 'there should be a balance' without saying where the balance lies or how it would be decided.
Presenting a counterargument in one sentence and dismissing it in the next without engaging it.
Using hypothetical students ('imagine a student who...') as the only evidence, with no grounding in reading, experience, or observation.
Ignoring practical complications (who supervises, who provides transport, how the work is assessed) that a thoughtful position would need to address.
Confusing a community project with ordinary group work or a single afternoon of volunteering, which misreads the long-term aspect of the prompt.

blueprint.theme: Education, community, and the purposes of practice versus experience.

Keep homework, add projects separately
Replace only where skills overlap

plan.theme: whether cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land and invite residents to harvest them

payload.title: Synthesis: Should Cities Plant Public Orchards for Residents to Harvest?

prompt.scenario: Across many towns and cities, parks departments are being asked to replace or supplement ordinary shade trees with fruit and nut trees on public land such as parks, school grounds, medians and sidewalk planting strips, and to invite residents to pick what grows. Supporters describe free food, shade and neighborly gatherings. Critics point to fallen fruit, wasps, maintenance costs, liability and the question of who actually ends up with the harvest. Others argue that the idea works only under particular conditions. Carefully read the six sources that follow, including the introductory information for each source.
prompt.task: Write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land and invite residents to harvest them.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position; a position may be in favor, opposed, or conditional (for example, supporting the practice only in certain locations or under certain arrangements).

Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning, and indicate clearly which sources you use by referring to them as Source A, Source B, and so on, or by the author's name.
Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning rather than merely summarizing or listing what the sources say; the sources are there to serve your argument, not to replace it.
Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

sources.title: Five Seasons In, Marlow Bend Weighs the Harvest on Orchard Boulevard
sources.attribution: Teodora Vask, staff reporter, The Pell River Ledger, 2024
sources.body:
When Marlow Bend replaced 340 dying ash trees along Orchard Boulevard with plums, pawpaws, hazelnuts and serviceberries in 2019, the city council called it the first edible street in the region. Five seasons later the branches are bearing, and so are the complaints.

The parks department logged 212 service requests related to the trees last year, most of them about fallen plums staining sidewalks and drawing wasps in late August. Yet the same department counted eleven neighborhood harvest days, organized by a volunteer group that calls itself the Boulevard Gleaners, which carried roughly 2,300 pounds of fruit to two church pantries before it could rot on the pavement.

"The trees that have a block captain look great," said parks superintendent Imani Threlkeld. "The ones that don't look like nobody loves them, because nobody does." Her department's figures show that a fruit tree on a block with a volunteer steward costs the city about 71 dollars a year to maintain, compared with 48 dollars for an ordinary shade tree and 112 dollars for a fruit tree on a block with no steward at all.

Council member Rufus Adebanjo-Lind, who voted for the program, now wants new plantings limited to parks and school grounds rather than sidewalks. "A plum tree over a bus stop was a mistake," he said. "A plum tree beside a playground is a gift." The council takes up his proposal next month, and both the Gleaners and a group of Orchard Boulevard shop owners have asked to speak.

sources.title: A Sidewalk Plum Is Not a Food Policy
sources.attribution: Corwin Ashby-Feld, opinion column, The Hollowmere Review, 2023
sources.body:
Every spring some council somewhere discovers the public orchard, and every spring I am asked to be charmed. I decline. The picture is lovely: a child on tiptoe, a grandmother with an apron full of pears, a street that feeds its own. The arithmetic is not.

A plum tree fruits for about three weeks. Hunger lasts fifty-two. A family that cannot afford groceries in February is not helped by a windfall in August that it has no way to can, freeze or store. What that family needs is money, refrigeration and a pantry that is open on Tuesdays, none of which grows on a branch.

Consider also who gets the fruit. Not the man in the wheelchair, who cannot reach it. Not the night-shift nurse, who sleeps through the two good picking days. The harvest goes to whoever has a ladder, a free Saturday and the nerve to strip a tree before the neighbors notice. We call that sharing. It looks more like a race.

Then comes the cleanup. Rotting fruit on a sidewalk is a slip hazard, a wasp buffet and, eventually, a claim against the city. A hazelnut dropped from twenty feet onto a parked windshield is a small event that produces a large letter. A city that cannot keep its ordinary maples pruned should not be volunteering to run an orchard.

Plant shade. Shade is free every year, falls on everyone equally and never needs a block captain. Then take the money you would have spent chasing plums down the gutter and give it to the food bank, which already knows what to do with it.

sources.title: Who Picks the Pears: A Conversation with Verrin Heights Parks Director Osric Palumbo
sources.attribution: Interview conducted by Nadira Quell for the Ostrander Institute for Urban Land oral history series, 2025
sources.body:
Quell: Your department has planted edible trees twice, with very different results. What happened?

Palumbo: In 2017 we put twelve pear trees in sidewalk cutouts downtown because a grant paid for them. Nobody on that street asked for them. They are the ugliest trees we own. Pears drop on the sidewalk, the merchants call us, and we send a crew with a hose. In 2021 a seniors' club at Thistle Park asked for a grove. We planted forty trees there, mostly persimmons, hazelnuts and serviceberries, and the club signed an agreement to water, pick and sweep. Those are the best trees we own.

Quell: So the difference is the people, not the trees?

Palumbo: Both. Species matters. A persimmon holds its fruit until someone takes it; a plum lets go the moment it ripens and finds the nearest shoe. We now plant only what I call polite fruit. But the agreement matters more. My rule is simple: no steward, no tree. If a group will not put its name on a two-page paper before the hole is dug, the hole does not get dug.

Quell: Critics say the harvest goes to whoever gets there first.

Palumbo: That is exactly what happens when nobody organizes it. At Thistle Park there is a chalkboard with picking dates, a shelf of loaner poles for people who cannot climb, and a standing rule that the first basket of the day goes to the pantry on Ferrow Street. None of that is complicated. All of it has to be decided before the first blossom, not after the first complaint.

Quell: Would you plant fruit trees along streets again?

Palumbo: Not in a tree pit, no. In a park, a schoolyard, a library lawn, yes, gladly, if someone has asked for it.
paragraphs: Quell: Your department has planted edible trees twice, with very different results.
What happened?
Palumbo: In 2017 we put twelve pear trees in sidewalk cutouts downtown because a grant paid for them.
Nobody on that street asked for them.
They are the ugliest trees we own.
Pears drop on the sidewalk, the merchants call us, and we send a crew with a hose.
In 2021 a seniors' club at Thistle Park asked for a grove.
We planted forty trees there, mostly persimmons, hazelnuts and serviceberries, and the club signed an agreement to water, pick and sweep.
Those are the best trees we own.
Quell: So the difference is the people, not the trees?
Palumbo: Both.
Species matters.
A persimmon holds its fruit until someone takes it; a plum lets go the moment it ripens and finds the nearest shoe.
We now plant only what I call polite fruit.
But the agreement matters more.
My rule is simple: no steward, no tree.
If a group will not put its name on a two-page paper before the hole is dug, the hole does not get dug.
Quell: Critics say the harvest goes to whoever gets there first.
Palumbo: That is exactly what happens when nobody organizes it.

At Thistle Park there is a chalkboard with picking dates, a shelf of loaner poles for people who cannot climb, and a standing rule that the first basket of the day goes to the pantry on Ferrow Street.
None of that is complicated.
All of it has to be decided before the first blossom, not after the first complaint.
Quell: Would you plant fruit trees along streets again?
Palumbo: Not in a tree pit, no.
In a park, a schoolyard, a library lawn, yes, gladly, if someone has asked for it.

sources.title: June, With Purple Fingers
sources.attribution: Lissette Marrow, personal essay, The Caddis Falls Almanac, 2024
sources.body:
The serviceberry outside the Caddis Falls branch library is not a remarkable tree. It is maybe fifteen feet tall, leans a little toward the bike rack, and for eleven months of the year nobody looks at it. Then June comes and it is the most important tree in the neighborhood.

My daughter was six the first time we picked. She did not believe me that the berries were food. Food, in her experience, arrived in a plastic clamshell with a sticker. I ate one in front of her. She watched me for a full minute to see if I would die, then ate four, then thirty.

That is where I met Mr. Haldane, who lives in the brick building and who had been picking that tree alone for nine years. He showed us how to bend a branch down without snapping it. He told us the berries were better with lemon. He had never spoken to me before and has not stopped since. I now know his knee is bad and his sister is in Ferndale and he does not care for the new bus route.

I will not pretend the tree is tidy. The berries stain the sidewalk, and for two weeks the birds hold a loud and messy festival in its branches. So does everything worth doing. My kitchen is a disaster after we bake. The library steps are a disaster after story hour.

What the tree gives is not really the fruit, though the fruit is good. It is the excuse. It gives a shy child and an old man a reason to stand on the same sidewalk and reach for the same branch. You cannot buy that in a clamshell. A city that plants it is planting something it will not be able to measure, which is not the same as saying it is not worth planting.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt ("Cities planting fruit trees has pros and cons"), only summarizes what the sources say, or takes no position the reader could disagree with. A thesis that merely announces the topic ("This essay will discuss public orchards") also earns 0.
descriptors.1: States a defensible, arguable position on whether cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land for residents to harvest. The position may be in favor, opposed, or conditional, but a conditional thesis must name the condition (for example, "only in parks and schoolyards with a signed steward group") rather than saying "it depends." The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: Defensible positions include: full support; opposition in favor of shade trees and direct food funding; support limited to parks, schoolyards and library lawns rather than sidewalks; support only where a volunteer steward group commits before planting; support for low-mess species only. A thesis that says the question "is complicated" without committing earns 0.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, offers only personal opinion with no reference to the sources, or uses material unrelated to the prompt.
descriptors.1: Mentions or quotes material from fewer than three sources, or from three sources in a way that is mostly summary with little or no explanation of how it supports a position. Commentary, where present, repeats the source's point in different words.
descriptors.2: Uses at least three sources, but the evidence is handled unevenly: some sources are explained in relation to the thesis while others are dropped in as quotations or listed one after another ("Source A says... Source B says..."). The line of reasoning is loose; paragraphs may be organized by source rather than by the writer's own claims. Numbers from Source E or F may be cited without saying what they show.
descriptors.3: Uses at least three sources as support for a clear line of reasoning organized around the writer's own claims. Commentary consistently explains how each piece of evidence advances the position, for example by connecting the stewardship cost gap in Source F to the low volunteer willingness in Source E. Some commentary may be thin or may not fully address evidence that cuts against the thesis.
descriptors.4: Uses at least three sources with specific, well-chosen evidence that is woven into a sustained line of reasoning. Commentary consistently and explicitly explains the significance of each piece of evidence to the thesis and shows how the sources relate to one another (agreement, tension, qualification). The writer puts sources in conversation, for example using Source C's "no steward, no tree" rule to answer Source B's fairness objection, or using Source E's gap between approval (68 percent for parks) and participation (23 percent harvested) to test Source D's claims. Counterevidence is acknowledged and handled rather than ignored.

rows.task_specific: Count a source as 'used' only if the essay draws specific content from it (a claim, quotation, figure or example), not merely its letter. Sources E and F count as used when the writer cites a specific number and interprets it. Uniting evidence across text and data sources (e.g. Source A's 71/48/112 figures match Source F) is a mark of the 3-4 range. A response that reaches 4 need not use all six sources; three well-integrated sources can earn 4.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Prose is adequate but the argument stays at the level of pro versus con, treats every source as equally reliable, or uses sweeping generalities and ornamental language without adding to the argument. Simply including a counterargument paragraph does not by itself earn the point.
descriptors.1: Demonstrates sophistication of thought in at least one sustained way: situating the argument in a broader context (what public land is for, who public goods actually reach); explaining the limits or implications of the position (for example, that a steward requirement may concentrate orchards in neighborhoods with organized residents); weighing the differing purposes and reliability of the sources (a personal essay versus a department cost report versus an op-ed with a clear agenda); or writing in a consistently vivid, precise and persuasive style that serves the argument.

rows.task_specific: Credit, for example, an essay that notices Source B's fairness objection and Source C's loaner poles address the same problem from opposite conclusions, or that observes Source E's 32 percent unsure about safety suggests education rather than planting is the limiting factor. Do not credit a mere list of 'both sides.'

scoring_notes: Score holistically within each row; a response need not do everything listed to earn a level, but must meet the core expectation of that level.
A conditional thesis that names its condition is fully defensible and should not be scored lower than a flat yes or no.

Misreading a number (for example, saying 68 percent of residents harvested when Source E says 23 percent) does not automatically lower the score, but commentary built on a misreading cannot count as effective evidence.
Organizing paragraphs by source rather than by claim is the most common marker of a 2 in Row B.
Row C is awarded for what the essay does throughout or at a key moment, not for a single sentence of hedging in the conclusion.

defensible_positions: Cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land and invite harvesting because the social and food benefits outweigh manageable mess and cost.
Cities should not plant edible trees on public land; they should plant shade trees and direct the savings to food banks and pantries that address hunger year-round.
Cities should plant edible trees only in parks, schoolyards and library lawns, not in sidewalk tree pits or over bus stops, where fallen fruit causes most complaints.
Cities should plant edible trees only where a resident group has formally committed to watering, picking and cleanup before the trees go in, since stewardship explains the cost gap.
Cities should proceed, but pair plantings with organized harvest systems (posted picking dates, loaner poles, pantry-first rules) so the fruit reaches people who cannot race for it.
lines_of_reasoning: Stewardship, not fruit itself, drives cost: Source F shows a stewarded fruit tree costs 71 dollars versus 112 unstewarded, so the policy question is really about organizing volunteers, which Source E suggests only 29 percent are willing to do.
Location determines outcome: Source A's council member, Source C's director and Source E's split (68 percent for parks, 41 percent for streets) converge on parks rather than sidewalks.

Equity cuts both ways: Source B argues the harvest goes to those with ladders and free Saturdays, while Source C shows that rule-setting (loaner poles, pantry-first baskets) can answer that objection.

Unmeasurable benefits still count: Source D's account of neighbors meeting over a tree, read against Source E's gap between approval and participation, raises the question of whether the benefit is food or community.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Source B's 'A plum tree fruits for about three weeks. Hunger lasts fifty-two.' compresses the op-ed's central claim that seasonal fruit cannot address year-round need.
Source A's council member contrasts the plum tree over a bus stop with the one beside a playground, giving writers a ready-made frame for a location-based position.
Source D's Mr. Haldane story makes the social benefit concrete, inviting writers to weigh narrative evidence against statistical evidence.
Source D admits the mess and answers it with 'So does everything worth doing,' modeling how a writer can concede a cost without abandoning a position.

source_uses.usable_for: Concrete program details (340 trees, 212 complaints, 2,300 pounds to pantries), the stewardship cost comparison, and a proposal to shift plantings from sidewalks to parks; usable by pro, con and conditional positions.

The strongest opposition: seasonality versus year-round hunger, unequal access to the harvest, liability and mess, and the alternative of shade trees plus food-bank funding; also a target for rebuttal.

The conditional case: contrast of unrequested sidewalk pears with a requested park grove, 'polite fruit' species choice, the 'no steward, no tree' rule, and organized harvest practices that answer fairness objections.
The social and intangible benefits (neighbors meeting, children learning where food comes from), an honest concession about mess, and a claim that unmeasurable goods still justify planting.

Public support that depends on location (68 percent parks versus 41 percent streets), the gap between approval and actual harvesting (23 percent), widespread worry about mess (57 percent), low volunteer willingness (29 percent) and uncertainty about safety (32 percent unsure).

Cost evidence: shade trees cost 48 dollars, stewarded fruit trees 71, unstewarded 112, nut trees 64 and 98; supports arguments that stewardship or species choice, not fruit itself, determines the burden, and that nut trees are cheaper than fruit trees.

common_pitfalls: Writing a thesis that says public orchards have 'advantages and disadvantages' without choosing a position.
Organizing the essay source by source (a paragraph on A, then B, then C) instead of around the writer's own claims.
Quoting Source D's warm anecdote without acknowledging that a personal essay about one tree is not evidence about a whole program.
Citing a number from Source E or F without saying what it demonstrates, or confusing approval of park plantings (68 percent) with willingness to volunteer (29 percent).
Treating Source B's op-ed as neutral fact rather than as an argument with its own rhetorical aims.
Ignoring the location distinction (sidewalk versus park) that runs through Sources A, C and E, which collapses the most useful conditional position into a simple pro or con.
Using the sources as decoration for an opinion formed in advance rather than letting them shape and complicate the position.

blueprint.theme: Public land, shared food and the conditions under which a community good actually reaches a community
blueprint.issue: Whether cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land and invite residents to harvest them
stances: In favor: plant edible trees broadly for food, shade and community
Opposed: plant shade trees instead and fund food banks directly
Conditional on location: parks, schoolyards and library lawns only, not sidewalks
Conditional on stewardship: only where a resident group commits before planting, with organized harvest rules
Species-based: plant only low-mess fruit and nut trees

devices.function: Source B sets a three-week fruiting season against fifty-two weeks of hunger to argue the policy is symbolic rather than substantive.
Source A pairs the bus-stop plum with the playground plum to crystallize the location argument.
Source D's encounter with Mr. Haldane supplies the community-building case in human terms.
Source D concedes mess and reframes it as the price of anything worthwhile.
Source C coins 'polite fruit' to define species that hold their fruit, giving writers a usable term for a species-based condition.
Source A's 71, 48 and 112 dollar figures, repeated in Source F, anchor the cost debate in consistent numbers.
