plan.theme: a veteran stage manager's talk to a high school crew about the value of work the audience never sees

payload.title: Rhetorical Analysis: Marisol Quade, "Where the Play Depends on You"

prompt.scenario: Speaker: Marisol Quade, a stage manager with thirty-one years of experience in regional and community theater. Audience: the eighteen-member student technical crew of Harrow Bend High School's spring production, gathered on the stage after the final dress rehearsal in April 2019. Exigence: the crew is tired and discouraged after a long rehearsal, and several students have complained that their work will go unnoticed on opening night. Purpose: to persuade the crew that unseen work is not lesser work, and that invisibility is the measure of their success, so they approach opening night with pride and focus.
prompt.task: The passage below is a talk given in April 2019 by Marisol Quade, a veteran stage manager, to the student technical crew of Harrow Bend High School on the night before their spring production opened. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Quade makes to convince the crew that the work an audience never sees is worth doing well.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices and can be defended with evidence from the passage.
Select and cite specific evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning, showing how the writer's choices work toward her purpose for this audience.

sources.title: Where the Play Depends on You
sources.attribution: Marisol Quade, remarks to the student technical crew of Harrow Bend High School, delivered on the stage after the final dress rehearsal, April 2019
paragraphs: (1) Thirty-one years ago I stood where you are standing, holding a roll of glow tape and wondering why I had signed up for a job nobody would clap for.
(2) Tomorrow night four hundred people will fill those seats, and not one of them will know your names.

(3) They will not see the forty feet of cable you coiled this afternoon, or the sandbag you re-tied twice because the first knot felt wrong, or the three-second hole in the second act that you closed with a flashlight and a whisper.
(4) Good.
(5) I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too.
(6) Why spend six weeks building a world for other people to stand in?
(7) Why learn the choreography of a scene change you perform in total darkness?
(8) The answer I would have given at seventeen was that someone had to do it.
(9) The answer I give now is different: the dark is not where the play hides from you; it is where the play depends on you.
(10) Let me tell you about a girl named Theodora Vance, who ran the fly rail for a production of a storm play at the old Carrow Street Playhouse in 1994.
(11) In the third act a painted sky was supposed to drop in on a count of eight.
(12) The actor jumped his cue by half a page, and the storm he was describing to the audience had not arrived.
(13) Theodora did not panic, did not wait for me, did not check the book.
(14) She brought the sky in on the line, early, perfectly, and the audience gasped at the weather.
(15) The review the next morning praised the actor's uncanny timing.
(16) Theodora read that review on the bus and, as she told me later, laughed until the driver asked if she was all right.
(17) That laugh is the whole job.
(18) A stage crew is the circulatory system of a production: nobody admires it, nobody photographs it, and the moment it stops, everything on the surface turns gray.
(19) The actors are the face; you are the pulse.
(20) Count what you have done this month: eleven set pieces, two hundred and six lighting cues, four quick changes timed under ninety seconds, one trapdoor that now closes without a sound.
(21) None of that is magic.
(22) All of it will look like magic.
(23) I will admit the arrangement is not fair, and I would be lying if I told you it never stung.
(24) There were years I wanted a bow.
(25) There was a night in Lissenbrook when the director thanked everyone by name at the cast party and skipped the booth entirely, and I drove home with the radio off.

(26) But here is what I understood by morning: the thanks I wanted was already in the room, spent before the curtain fell, in every second the audience forgot they were sitting in a building with a roof.
(27) Applause is for what was seen.
(28) Invisibility is the proof that you did it right.
(29) So tomorrow, when the house lights dim and the first cue goes, listen.
(30) You will hear four hundred people stop breathing at once, and you will know that you are the reason.
(31) No one will ever thank you for it.
(32) Thank each other.
(33) Then check your headset, and let's go.
sources.stance: Unseen technical work is the foundation of a performance, and going unnoticed is proof of doing it well.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Quade uses rhetorical choices to convince the crew'), only summarizes the talk, or makes a claim about theater rather than about Quade's rhetoric.
descriptors.1: A defensible claim about how Quade's choices work toward persuading the crew that unseen work matters. The claim may name specific choices (the Theodora anecdote, the circulatory-system metaphor, the admission of unfairness) or may characterize her overall approach (for example, that she reframes invisibility from a loss into an achievement), but it must be something the essay could argue and support.

rows.task_specific: A thesis that identifies a purpose other than the one in the prompt is acceptable if it is defensible from the passage (for example, that Quade aims to steady a tired crew before opening night). A list of devices with no claim about how they function does not earn the point.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the talk, or offers evidence with no connection to any claim.
descriptors.1: Mostly summary or general statements about the passage; quotations, if any, are not tied to a specific rhetorical choice or to Quade's purpose.
descriptors.2: Cites specific sentences and names choices accurately, but commentary stays at the level of labeling ('she uses an anecdote to connect with the audience') or repeats what the quotation says without explaining why that choice suits this crew on this night.
descriptors.3: Cites specific evidence for several choices and explains how each one helps Quade persuade the crew, with a line of reasoning that mostly holds together. Some commentary may be uneven, or the essay may treat the choices as a list rather than showing how they build on one another.
descriptors.4: Cites specific, well-chosen evidence and consistently explains how each choice works on this particular audience of discouraged students the night before opening. The essay traces a line of reasoning across the talk, for example showing how the rhetorical questions in sentences 6 and 7 voice the crew's doubt, how the anecdote and metaphor answer that doubt, how the concession in sentences 23 to 26 earns trust by admitting the cost, and how the closing commands convert the argument into action.

rows.task_specific: Choices that count include: the opening ethos appeal (1); the ironic 'Good' and sentence-length variation (3 to 4); rhetorical questions that voice the crew's doubts (6 to 7); the antithesis and colon in sentence 9; the Theodora anecdote and its ironic review (10 to 16); the circulatory-system metaphor and face/pulse antithesis (18 to 19); the enumeration of concrete work (20); the paired antithesis of sentences 21 to 22; the concession and rebuttal, including the Lissenbrook memory, in 23 to 28; the tone shift from confessional to rallying at 29; direct commands and the final juxtaposition of 31 and 32. Commentary must connect the choice to the audience's situation (students, tired, feeling unseen) and to the purpose, not simply to 'the reader.'

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Commentary stays within the choices as isolated items; general praise of Quade's writing; or elevated vocabulary without added insight.
descriptors.1: The essay does at least one of the following consistently: explains how the rhetorical situation shapes Quade's choices (why a veteran admitting her own resentment is more persuasive to teenagers than a simple pep talk); traces a tension in the talk, such as the way Quade both insists invisibility is a reward and admits it stings; shows how the argument accumulates, for example how the Theodora anecdote, the metaphor, and the concession each redefine what 'thanks' means until sentence 32 offers the crew a substitute; or writes with controlled, precise prose throughout.

rows.task_specific: Observing that the talk ends with practical instructions ('check your headset') rather than a grand flourish, and explaining why that understatement fits a speaker who values unseen work, is one route to this point.

scoring_notes: Essays that misidentify a device (calling the circulatory-system comparison a simile) are not penalized if the commentary on its effect is accurate.
Paragraph-by-paragraph summary with occasional device names earns at most 2 on Row B.

An essay that discusses only one choice in depth can earn a 3 on Row B if the commentary is specific and tied to purpose, but a 4 requires more than one choice and a line of reasoning across the passage.
Do not reward length; a short essay with precise commentary on three choices outscores a long essay that lists eight.
The sophistication point is not earned by a sweeping conclusion about the importance of teamwork or by using the word 'juxtaposition' without explaining the effect.

defensible_positions: Quade reframes invisibility from a loss into evidence of success by voicing the crew's doubts, answering them with a concrete story and a bodily metaphor, and then admitting the cost before converting the argument into a closing instruction.
Quade builds credibility by positioning herself as a former doubter and a once-slighted crew member, so that her praise of unseen work reads as earned rather than sentimental.
Quade moves the crew from discouragement to readiness through a shift from question and anecdote to confession and command.
lines_of_reasoning: Doubt voiced (6 to 7), doubt answered by example (10 to 16), answer generalized by metaphor (18 to 22), objection conceded and overturned (23 to 28), argument turned into action (29 to 33).
Three redefinitions of 'thanks': the review that credits the wrong person (15), the thanks 'already in the room' (26), and the instruction to thank each other (32).
Credibility built by shared experience: Quade stood where they stand (1), thought what they think (5), wanted what they want (24), and still chose the booth.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Establishes Quade as someone who once held the same doubts in the same position, so the crew hears her as a peer who stayed rather than an authority lecturing them.
A long inventory of unseen tasks is cut off by the single word 'Good,' which jolts the crew by treating the thing they fear as the goal.
Welcoming invisibility, the review that credits the actor, and work that is not magic but looks like it all train the crew to read lack of credit as a sign of success.
Puts the crew's unspoken complaint into Quade's own mouth so she can answer it instead of dismissing it.
Balanced oppositions (hides/depends, face/pulse, applause/invisibility) make her reframing sound like a settled truth rather than consolation.
Colons set up each key claim as a revelation, slowing the crew down right before the line she most wants remembered.
A specific, named crew member saving a show and laughing at the misdirected praise gives the crew a model of how to feel, not just what to believe.
The tripled 'did not' conveys Theodora's composure and implicitly lists the instincts the crew must suppress tomorrow.
Comparing the crew to the circulatory system makes invisibility a property of vital things rather than unimportant ones, and 'pulse' gives them a dignified role opposite the actors' 'face.'

Concrete numbers drawn from the crew's own month make the argument about their work rather than about crews in general, and the silent trapdoor shows that their best work is defined by what the audience will not notice.
Admitting that going unthanked stings, with a specific memory of the slighted booth, prevents the talk from sounding naive and makes the rebuttal about thanks 'already in the room' more trustworthy.
The short confession and the drive home with the radio off let the crew see their own hurt reflected in a veteran, which lowers their defenses before the turn.
The voice moves from confessional to brisk and commanding, carrying the crew out of reflection and into the readiness opening night requires.
Second-person commands make the crew participants rather than listeners and end the talk as a cue rather than a speech.
Setting 'No one will ever thank you' directly against 'Thank each other' gives the crew a substitute for the applause they will not get.
Ending with a routine headset check rather than a flourish enacts the talk's own value: the important thing is the quiet, practical work.

source_uses.usable_for: All evidence for the rhetorical analysis essay.

common_pitfalls: Treating the talk as an essay about theater and arguing whether crew work is valued, rather than analyzing how Quade argues.
Listing devices paragraph by paragraph with the same generic effect ('this makes the audience feel connected') for each.
Ignoring the audience: forgetting that the listeners are tired high school students, which is why Quade uses their own inventory of work in sentence 20 and ends with a plain instruction.
Quoting sentence 18 and labeling it a metaphor without explaining why 'circulatory system' (vital, invisible, fatal if it stops) is a fitting comparison for her purpose.
Overlooking the concession in paragraph five or treating it as a weakness in the argument rather than as a deliberate credibility move.
Claiming the anecdote is 'pathos' without explaining what the laugh on the bus is meant to teach the crew about how to feel when the credit goes elsewhere.

blueprint.theme: The value of unseen labor and the redefinition of recognition
blueprint.issue: Whether work that an audience never notices is worth doing with full commitment
stances: Invisibility is the proof of a crew's success, not a slight.
Credit matters and withholding it is unfair, a view Quade concedes before overturning.

devices.function: Positions the speaker as a former doubter who shares the crew's situation.
Long catalogue followed by one-word sentence to surprise and reframe.
Treats lack of credit as the desired outcome.
Voices the crew's doubts so they can be answered.
Compresses the reframing into memorable oppositions.
Colons stage each key claim as a revelation.
Concrete story of a crew member whose save was credited to an actor, modeling the right response.
Tripled negation conveys composure under pressure.
Circulatory system and face/pulse make invisibility a mark of vital work.
Concrete counts of the crew's own work ground the argument.
Admits unfairness and personal hurt before redefining thanks.
Personal memory of being skipped at the cast party invites identification.
Moves from confessional to rallying command.
Second-person commands turn listeners into participants.
Sets no thanks against mutual thanks to offer a substitute for applause.
Plain practical ending enacts the value of quiet work.

plan.theme: the extent to which a neighborhood should share responsibility for maintaining its public sidewalks and steps

payload.title: Whose Step Is It? Shared Responsibility for Public Sidewalks and Stairs

prompt.scenario: In a column for a small-town weekly, commentator Delia Marchbank wrote the following about the hillside stairways and sidewalks that connect the streets of her town.
prompt.task: Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which the residents of a neighborhood should share responsibility for maintaining the public sidewalks and steps that run through it.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning, drawing on your reading, experience, or observations.
Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning, and use appropriate strategies to develop and organize your argument.

sources.title: Nobody's Child
sources.attribution: Delia Marchbank, column in the Fallow Ridge Weekly Courier
sources.body: In many hillside towns, the stairs and sidewalks that stitch one street to the next are nobody's child. The city claims them on its maps and forgets them in its budget; the people who live beside them sweep the leaves off some mornings and step over the broken risers on others. Some residents argue that the fix is obvious: if you live on a block, you owe it your shovel, your rake, and a Saturday now and then. Others answer that this is exactly what taxes are for, and that asking neighbors to patch public concrete lets officials off the hook while quietly penalizing the elderly, the renters, and the people working two jobs. A third camp says the truth sits in the middle: neighbors should keep things passable, but anything involving rebar is the city's problem. Who, in the end, owns a public step?

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that merely restates the prompt (for example, 'Neighbors and the city both have a role'), summarizes Marchbank's three camps without choosing, or takes a position on a different question (such as whether taxes are too high).
descriptors.1: States a defensible position on how much responsibility residents should bear for public sidewalks and steps. The position may be absolute, qualified, or conditional, but it must commit to a claim a reader could dispute. A thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: Qualified theses count fully as long as they draw a real line: for example, 'residents should handle routine upkeep but never structural repair,' or 'shared upkeep is fair only where the city first makes the infrastructure safe.' A thesis that says 'it depends on the situation' without naming what it depends on does not earn the point.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, repeats the stimulus, or offers only general statements with no evidence.
descriptors.1: Offers evidence that is mostly general or unrelated to the claim (for instance, listing things that are wrong with towns), with little or no explanation of how it supports the position. Commentary, if present, simply asserts that the evidence proves the point.
descriptors.2: Provides some specific evidence (an observed block, a remembered snowstorm, a passage from reading, a plausible scenario) but the explanation is uneven: some evidence is linked to the claim, some is just dropped in, and the essay tends to list examples rather than build a line of reasoning.
descriptors.3: Provides specific, relevant evidence and explains how most of it supports the writer's position. The essay follows a recognizable line of reasoning (for example, moving from who benefits, to who can pay, to what fairness requires), though one or two links may be thin or one key objection may go unaddressed.
descriptors.4: Provides specific, well-chosen evidence and consistently explains how each piece advances the line of reasoning. The reasoning is organized so that each step depends on the one before it, and the writer accounts for the strongest competing view (such as the burden on renters, the elderly, or people working multiple jobs, or conversely the slowness and unreliability of municipal repair) and shows why the position still holds or how it is adjusted to meet the objection.

rows.task_specific: Acceptable evidence includes personal observation of a block or building, experience with volunteer or civic work, historical or literary examples of commons and shared upkeep, hypothetical but concrete scenarios, and reasoning from principles of fairness, safety, or liability. Evidence need not be factual in the statistical sense; it must be specific and tied to the claim. Do not reward essays for quoting Marchbank at length; the stimulus is a springboard, not a source to be analyzed.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Argument stays at the level of a single idea repeated, treats the question as a simple yes or no, or uses ornate language that does not advance the thought. Merely mentioning that 'both sides have a point' does not earn the point.
descriptors.1: Demonstrates complexity in one or more of these ways: distinguishes kinds of maintenance (sweeping, salting, patching, rebuilding) or kinds of residents (owners, renters, landlords, businesses) and shows how the answer shifts across them; explores a tension the position creates (for example, that volunteer upkeep can let a city quietly disinvest, or that strict municipal control can make a block feel like no one's); situates the question in a broader idea of what public space is for; or sustains a prose style that is controlled, precise, and persuasive throughout.

rows.task_specific: The sophistication point most often comes from an essay that explains the limits of its own position: who it would unfairly burden, what would happen if everyone followed it, or how it depends on a city holding up its end. Award it for insight embedded in the argument, not for a closing paragraph that gestures at nuance.

scoring_notes: Score the whole essay holistically within each row; do not deduct for a single weak paragraph if the essay as a whole meets the descriptor.
A position that residents should bear no responsibility beyond paying taxes is fully defensible and should be scored on its reasoning, not on whether the grader agrees.

An essay that argues a related but different question (for example, whether volunteering is good in general) can still earn Row A if it commits to a claim about sidewalks and steps somewhere, but Row B evidence must bear on the actual question.
Length is not a criterion. A short essay with a tight line of reasoning can earn 3 or 4 in Row B.
Essays that spend most of their space analyzing Marchbank's rhetoric rather than arguing a position usually cap at 2 in Row B.

defensible_positions: Residents should take substantial responsibility for routine upkeep because they benefit most directly and because waiting for the city means the steps never get fixed.
Residents owe nothing beyond what they already pay in taxes; shifting labor onto neighbors is a disguised cut in public service that falls hardest on those least able to carry it.
Responsibility should be divided by kind of work: residents keep the way passable (sweeping, salting, reporting hazards), and the city handles anything structural.
Shared responsibility is fair only after the city has brought the infrastructure to a safe baseline; before that, volunteer upkeep rewards neglect.
The question of who owns the step matters less than who organizes the work: block associations or landlords, not individual residents, should be the unit of responsibility.
Shared upkeep is worth embracing not for efficiency but because the act of caring for a shared stair is what turns a street into a neighborhood, even if it is less fair in the narrow sense.
lines_of_reasoning: Benefit and proximity: those who use a path daily notice problems first, can act fastest, and have the strongest stake; therefore a share of responsibility rightly belongs to them, with the city reserved for what neighbors cannot do.

Fairness and capacity: responsibility should track ability to carry it; since residents differ enormously in time, health, and tenure, a universal duty is regressive and the only fair collector is the tax system.

Division by scale: distinguish routine upkeep from capital repair, and argue that the line between them (roughly, anything a hardware store can supply versus anything needing an engineer) is where resident responsibility ends.

Incentives and moral hazard: whatever residents reliably do, officials will stop funding; therefore neighbors should either refuse structural work on principle or pair their labor with public pressure so that volunteering does not become a permanent subsidy.

Civic formation: shared maintenance builds the habits and acquaintance that make a block capable of other collective action, so it should be encouraged even where a purely municipal solution would be more efficient.

Counterintuitive: the most responsible thing residents can do is not to fix the steps themselves but to document and report them relentlessly, because informal repairs hide the scale of the problem and may create liability for the person who made them.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Calling the stairs 'nobody's child' frames the issue as one of neglect and belonging rather than engineering, inviting arguments about ownership and care.
The closing question leaves the issue open and hands the decision to the student, signaling that any of the three camps or a new one can be argued.

source_uses.usable_for: Springboard only: students may borrow the three camps as a map of positions, pick up the fairness objection in sentence 4, or push against the middle position in sentence 5, but they must supply their own evidence.

common_pitfalls: Writing a thesis that simply names all three camps from the stimulus and declares that each has merit, without committing to a line.
Treating 'maintenance' as one thing, so that the essay never distinguishes between sweeping leaves and rebuilding a collapsed stair.
Offering only abstract evidence ('communities are stronger when people help') with no concrete block, scene, or example.
Ignoring the fairness objection in the stimulus (the elderly, renters, people working two jobs) and so leaving the strongest counterargument unanswered.
Drifting into a general essay about taxes, government waste, or volunteerism and losing the specific question of public sidewalks and steps.
Spending the essay analyzing the column's language instead of using it as a springboard for an argument.
Ending with a vague call to 'work together' that retreats from the position argued in the body.

blueprint.issue: How much responsibility residents of a neighborhood should bear, alongside or instead of the city, for maintaining public sidewalks and hillside steps.
blueprint.theme: community, public space, and the division of labor between citizens and government
stances: Residents owe substantial labor to the public paths they use.
Maintenance is the city's job and residents owe only their taxes.
Residents handle routine upkeep; the city handles structural repair.
Shared responsibility is conditional on the city meeting a baseline first.

devices.function: Frames neglected infrastructure as an abandoned child, making the question emotional and moral as well as practical.
Sets the city's map against its budget and residents' sweeping against their stepping over, exposing that neither party fully acts.
Shovel, rake, and a Saturday make the first camp's demand concrete and modest-sounding.
Voices the fairness objection and the risk of letting officials off the hook, giving students a ready counterargument to answer.
Introduces a dividing line (passable versus rebar) that models how a qualified position can be made specific.
Leaves ownership unresolved so the student must decide.
